questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: I wanted to grow as a person and challenge my comfort zone. I also wanted to try living abroad in my life, and exchange is a fairly easy way of achieving that.

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The host university needed to be decent. The course selection had to suit me somewhat. The surrounding area needed to be decent, and it needed to be an English-speaking country.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It would be an 9 or 10/10 were it not for Covid. The hassle with the study permit, travel restrictions, cancelled events etc. due to Covid sucked. But it's quite telling when I still feel like I got an 8/10 experience, even with those problems. Exchange was awesome!!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Regarding UBC, it was easy enough. Regarding Covid, it was a pain. I spent many, many hours looking into restrictions, calling hotlines etc. Especially regarding travel restrictions and quarantine at arrival in Canada.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I didn't get assistance, but Go Global is there for exchange students. You can just drop into their office.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Help was there if needed.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Exchange students either get assigned to Walter Gage or Fairview Crescent. Walter Gage are three huge towers with 6-man flats. Fairview Crescent is village-like with small houses/flats for 4 to 6 people. Both are located fairly well regarding the rest of campus, with Gage being the closest to everything.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: At both Gage and Fairview, there is a kitchen with stove, oven, microwave and dishwasher. There's also some meal plan option, but I hear it sucks and is overpriced. Don't look into it, just cook.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There's nothing in the flats besides basic furniture. You need to buy all the kitchen equipment, bedding etc. Be prepared for that when you arrive at the dorm.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I lived at Fairview, which was OK. But the walls are thin with NO sound insulation, and the same applies to the doors. The windows are also single-paned, giving no thermal or sound insulation. It seemed better at Gage.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The courses do not follow set time slots like UCPH Science does, e.g. Monday 8-12 and Wednesday 8-17. Instead the "sections" for each course are spread a bit randomly throughout the week. It means there can be conflicts quite easily between courses, where you e.g. have a lecture in each simultaneously. Watch out for that. UBC does not provide an easy way to review this, so I personally made an Excel sheet and filled in each possible combination of courses to see how my week would look.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You browsed the course catalogue for 10 courses you wanted. This was submitted to Go Global as a priority list of 10, and they applied for you. This is because, as exchange students, we are not fully in the system and they thus need to apply for us. For some courses, Go Global could not register for you, and you had to consult the course teachers once the term started. You had until 14 days into the term to get the courses you wanted, where you could also drop out of the courses you wanted with no consequences.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Go Global could offer a lot of assistance.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Start browsing the course catalogue early. Plan your week regarding sections - it's e.g. a pain to have a single lecture at 16 when your day otherwise ended at 11. As an extension of that, make sure that combinations of different courses don't result in big conflicts. It would e.g. suck to have two lectures at the same time.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very good course selection - much more varied than UCPH.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: They were generally easier than UCPH courses, at least the courses I had. But it generally depends on the course and the teacher - I had friends in Engineering that struggled with their courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The lectures are really short - about 45 minutes. You also have to be on top of the course throughout the semester, as there are quizzes, assignments etc. throughout the course that actually factor into your final grade. It's not just all about the final exam.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
BIOL421: Plant-Microbe Interactions
MICB301: Microbial Ecophysiology
MICB405: Bioinformatics

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: BIOL421 was great if you're into plant biology and research methods. The teachers are great, especially Jim Kronstad. And the course is easy too.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Buying all the stuff for the dorm. Both kitchen equipment and bedding. But the kitchen stuff isn't that bad if you can split with your flatmates.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries are more expensive. Alcohol is a LOT more expensive - which is especially bad news as a Dane. Sugary stuff was much cheaper, and eating out was a bit less expensive than Copenhagen.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A LOT of things. A huge variety of clubs within whatever hobby, sports games to come watch (tickets being free for students), drop-in sessions for skating, swimming etc. It really was a great selection, and the facilities are excellent.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to the sports games, and join a club or two!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Sightsee and hike! And in the mid-term break, try to go somewhere else in North America - e.g. Hawaii or Toronto.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Don't be afraid to ask questions - in most cases, it leads into good conversation. Just initiate!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The tipping culture. It was just an odd thing you always needed to think about - how much to tip, whether to tip, where to tip...

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendliness towards strangers, and how open people were for talk.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1: Go to the campus events, e.g. sports games! 2: Invest in or bring hiking boots - experience the nature! 3: Eat out a lot!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you don't get on-campus housing, try to find something in Kitsilano. A lot of students live in basement suites, which are subletted by the house owners. Try finding a few other people to share a suite with.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Growing as a person. I had to talk to a lot of people I didn't know, which is outside of my comfort zone. I feel like I'm more "worldly" too, in part because I met so many exchange students from across the world, in part because I learned about Canadian/North American culture.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Settling in and taking care of a lot of small things. Finding a mobile plan, buying kitchen equipment for the dorm, learning how course grading works...

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: If you have any doubts about going: don't. Trust me - it's worth the money, it's worth the hassle, and it's worth missing courses at UCPH. It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity and experience. I will never regret doing it, and I'm positive you won't either.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
